Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Vignette:
For fifty-eight years, Margaret had lived a life that was, by her own description, orderly and predictable. She and her husband, Frank, a retired postal worker, had settled into a comfortable rhythm in their small bungalow on a quiet street in Ohio. That rhythm ended on a Tuesday afternoon in late October, three years ago. Frank had been on his way back from the hardware store, a simple errand he’d run a thousand times. Margaret was in the kitchen when she heard the sound. It wasn’t the screech of brakes or the crunch of metal she had imagined when she’d thought of car accidents. What she heard was a wet, percussive thud, followed by a long, low hiss of steam. She ran to the front door and saw the scene at the intersection: a sedan, its front end crumpled against the driver’s side of Frank’s old pickup. The air smelled of hot rubber, gasoline, and something else—a sharp, sweet chemical odor she later learned was the coolant from the ruptured radiator. That smell, more than any image, had lodged itself in her.

The paramedics arrived, the ambulance’s siren dying into a low, rhythmic wail as it pulled up. She remembers the frantic, impersonal efficiency of it all, the way she was gently but firmly pushed back from the scene by a young officer. She watched them load Frank onto a gurney, his face a mask of blood and confusion. He died at the hospital two hours later from internal bleeding. Margaret did not cry that day. She felt as though she had been encased in a thick layer of glass, able to see the world but unable to touch it.

In the months that followed, the glass began to crack, but not into a release of grief. Instead, it fractured into a series of sharp, jagged shards of fear. The first anniversary of the accident arrived, and Margaret found herself unable to leave the house. She had come to believe that the date itself was a kind of trap, a day when the universe repeated its cruelties. She drew the curtains and sat in the dark, her heart hammering at every passing car. She stopped driving entirely. The sight of a damaged car, even one with a minor dent, would make her stomach clench. She would cross the street or turn around and go the other way to avoid walking past a body shop. Her world began to shrink.

The most persistent intrusions were not visual but olfactory. She would be folding laundry or washing dishes, and suddenly the air would thicken with the smell of hot rubber and sweet coolant. It was not a memory; it was a transport. She would be back on the front lawn, the hiss of the radiator filling her ears, the panic fresh and raw. These olfactory flashbacks came without warning. A whiff of car exhaust on a cold morning, the scent of a freshly paved road—any of these could instantly hijack her mind, leaving her disoriented and trembling for hours. At night, sleep was a battleground. She would lie awake, listening for the sounds of the neighborhood, her mind replaying a loop of the thud, the hiss, the silence. When she did drift off, she was plagued by fragmented, disjointed dreams that she could never fully recall, leaving her with a sense of dread that felt more real than the daylight.

She developed a rigid set of rituals to manage her terror. Every night, she would check every window and door in the house three times, sliding the deadbolts home with a satisfying click. She checked the locks on her car, which sat unused in the driveway, as a matter of course. Any unexpected movement—a bird darting past the window, her own cat padding silently into the room—would make her cry out and flinch, her body braced for a blow. She knew, intellectually, that there was no threat. But her body no longer believed her. When she tried to deliberately remember the details of that day, the sequence of events felt slippery and inaccessible, as if a fog had rolled in over the most critical moments. She could recall the smell, the sound, the officer’s face, but she could not hold the whole picture in her mind at once. The memory existed only as a series of ambush attacks.

Her unemployment became a problem in its own right. With no job to force her out of the house, her avoidance became total. Her daughter, who lived two states away, called every Sunday. Margaret would tell her she was fine, that she was keeping busy. She was not. She was sitting in her dark living room, watching the clock, waiting for the next ambush. What finally brought her to seek help was a simple, terrifying realization: she had not been to the grocery store in three weeks. She was running out of food, and the thought of walking past the intersection, of seeing a car, of smelling anything that might trigger the memory, was more powerful than her hunger. She called her doctor, her voice a thin, strained whisper, and said she needed to talk to someone. She is terrified that she will never feel safe again, but a smaller, quieter part of her is hoping that she might at least learn to walk to the end of her own driveway without seeing Frank’s face in every passing headlight.
